one_line: A NACHT-domain NLR family protein, distantly related to NLRC5, possibly involved in innate immunity.
summary: It belongs to the NOD-like receptor (NLR) family. This rests on its NACHT domain (Pfam) and a strong jackhmmer hit from the human NLRP3 seed (round 5, E-value 6e-193). Its Swiss-Prot match, mouse NLRC5 at 26% identity over 64% of the protein, gives the family but not the exact gene. No leucine-rich repeat domain was detected, and the immune roles listed (MHC class I regulation, interferon signalling) are known for mouse NLRC5, not tested here. The weak FANTASIA hint (inflammation-related GO terms) fits an immune role. It sits in a large cluster of 49 NLRC5-like Botryllus proteins, which matches the expanded NLR repertoire known in tunicates.
confidence_reason: The NLR family assignment is solid, but at 26% identity no specific gene or immune function can be carried over.

name_verdict.reason: The proposed name only adds "-like" to the header name NLRC5, and both rest on the same weak mouse NLRC5 match (26% identity). The evidence supports NLR family membership rather than true NLRC5 orthology, so the "-like" form is preferred.

one_line: A core histone H4 that packages DNA into nucleosomes.
summary: It is histone H4, based on 100% identity over its full length to Oikopleura dioica histone H4 (Swiss-Prot). Its 103-residue length fits H4. H4 is a core histone: it forms nucleosomes with H2A, H2B and H3 and is heavily modified by acetylation and methylation. The Pfam hits (CENP-T_C, TAF) are histone-fold domains, so they fit a histone. It belongs to a cluster of 18 similar Botryllus histone genes, which is typical of multicopy histone genes.
confidence_reason: An identical full-length match to a histone H4, a protein that barely varies between species, makes the function clear.

name_verdict.reason: The header name HIST1H3D is a histone H3 gene, but the sequence is identical to histone H4 over its full length. The proposed name H4.1 is correct but is an Oikopleura gene label, so the plain name "Histone H4" is recommended.

one_line: A NACHT-domain NOD-like receptor family protein, possibly an innate immune sensor; exact vertebrate counterpart unclear.
summary: It belongs to the NLR family. This rests on its NACHT domain (Pfam) and a strong jackhmmer hit from the human NLRP3 seed (round 5, E-value 4e-163). Its Swiss-Prot match, mouse NLRC5 at 26% identity over 56% of the protein, gives only the family. FANTASIA, a weak hint with no alignment behind it, points to mouse NLRP10 instead. No pyrin (PYD), CARD or LRR domain was detected, so the evidence cannot place it in the NLRC or NLRP subfamily. A role in innate immunity or inflammation is likely for the family, but has not been shown for this protein.
confidence_reason: Family membership is well supported, but weak identity and conflicting nearest hits leave the specific function unknown.

name_verdict.reason: The header name NLRP12 has no direct support on the sheet. The proposed NLRC5-like rests on a 26% identity match, and FANTASIA points to NLRP10. Both are NLR family names that the evidence cannot tell apart, so the family name is recommended.

one_line: A cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase of the PDE4 family that breaks down cAMP to end cAMP signalling.
summary: It is a PDE4-family cAMP phosphodiesterase. This rests on its Swiss-Prot match, mouse PDE4D at 64% identity over 54% of the protein, and its PDEase_I catalytic domain (Pfam). Like PDE4 enzymes, it likely uses metal ions to hydrolyse cAMP to AMP, controlling cAMP signalling in the cytoplasm and at membranes. The unmatched part of the protein is probably a regulatory N-terminal region that differs between isoforms. Tunicates split from vertebrates before PDE4A-D arose, so this one gene probably corresponds to the whole PDE4 family, not to PDE4D in particular.
confidence_reason: High identity over the catalytic region and a matching Pfam domain support the enzyme activity, though not a specific paralog.

name_verdict.reason: The header name pde-4 is the C. elegans name for the single PDE4 gene, which fits a tunicate gene that matches the whole PDE4 family. The proposed Pde4d names one vertebrate paralog, which 64% identity over half the protein cannot single out from PDE4A-D.

one_line: A peroxin-5 family receptor that likely brings PTS1-tagged proteins into peroxisomes.
summary: It is a PEX5 family protein. This rests on its Swiss-Prot match, Xenopus PEX5 at 34% identity over the full protein (E-value 2e-99), and on three TPR repeats (Pfam). TPR repeats are the part of PEX5 that binds the PTS1 targeting signal. Like PEX5, it likely binds PTS1-tagged proteins in the cytosol, carries them to the peroxisomal membrane for import into the matrix, and is then recycled. At 34% identity the family is clear, but the exact function is inferred rather than shown.
confidence_reason: A full-length match at moderate identity plus TPR repeats support the PEX5 family, but the identity is too low to be sure of the exact role.

name_verdict.reason: The best match is PEX5 itself (Xenopus pex5.S, 34% identity over the full length). Nothing on the sheet supports the vertebrate paralog PEX5L, an HCN channel subunit that does not act in peroxisome import. "pex5.S" is only a Xenopus label for one gene copy, so the plain name PEX5 is recommended.

one_line: Probable sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter of the SLC5A8/SLC5A12 group in the sodium:solute symporter family.
summary: Its best Swiss-Prot match is bovine SLC5A12 (SMCT2) at 33.5% identity over 92% of the protein. It also carries a sodium:solute symporter (SSF) Pfam domain. Together these suggest a plasma-membrane transporter that moves monocarboxylates such as lactate together with sodium. At this identity the match gives the family, not the gene. A single tunicate gene may correspond to both vertebrate SLC5A8 and SLC5A12, and the 14-member Botryllus cluster shows this group has expanded, so the exact substrate and paralog are uncertain.
confidence_reason: A near full-length match at 33.5% identity and a matching Pfam domain support the transporter family, but not the substrate or the exact gene.

name_verdict.reason: The proposed name SLC5A12 rests on a bovine SLC5A12 match at only 33.5% identity. The header name SLC5A8 names the closely related paralog and has no recorded evidence. Both genes are sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporters, and the evidence cannot tell them apart in a tunicate.

one_line: T-complex protein 11 family member of unknown precise function, related to TCP11 and TCP11L2.
summary: It carries a Tcp11 Pfam domain. Its best Swiss-Prot match is bovine TCP11L2 at 32.7% identity over 88% of the protein. This places it in the TCP11 family. Vertebrate members of this family are linked to the cytoskeleton and signaling (TCP11L2) or to sperm function (TCP11), but these GO terms come from the matched protein and were not measured here. Its function in Botryllus is uncertain.
confidence_reason: The family assignment is solid, but family members differ in function and identity is only 32.7%, so no specific function can be transferred.

name_verdict.reason: The proposed name TCP11L2 comes from a match at 32.7% identity. That level gives the family, not the paralog. The header name TCP11 is another member of the same family and has no recorded evidence. One tunicate gene may correspond to several vertebrate TCP11 paralogs.

one_line: Probable class A G protein-coupled receptor, distantly related to leucine-rich repeat-containing glycoprotein hormone/relaxin receptors.
summary: Two 7tm_1 Pfam hits mark it as a rhodopsin-family (class A) GPCR in the cell membrane. Its best Swiss-Prot match is the snail receptor GRL101, an LGR-type receptor, at 25.1% identity over 82% of the protein. One member of its MMseqs2 cluster is named RXFP2, which suggests it belongs to the LGR/relaxin receptor group. No leucine-rich repeat domain was detected, and its ligand is unknown.
confidence_reason: The 7tm_1 domains support a GPCR well, but the 25% identity match gives only a distant subfamily hint and no ligand.

name_verdict.reason: Neither 'GPROTEIN' nor 'G-like' is a gene name. 'G-like' seems to be a truncated form of the GRL101 description. The 7tm_1 domains and the distant GRL101 match support a class A GPCR, possibly of the LGR type.

one_line: Large macrodomain-PARP protein similar to PARP14, likely an ADP-ribosyltransferase that reads and writes ADP-ribose.
summary: It has nine Macro domains, two PARP catalytic domains and four RRM_PARP14_3 domains. This architecture matches the macro-PARP group, and the RRM_PARP14_3 domains point to PARP14 in particular. Its best Swiss-Prot match is human PARP14 at 26.5% identity over 66% of the protein. Human PARP14 is a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase that regulates interferon/STAT signaling and innate immunity, but in Botryllus that role is only inferred. The unusual number of domains may reflect a lineage-specific expansion or a merged gene model. It is not known whether its PARP domains are catalytically active.
confidence_reason: The domain composition and a long PARP14 match support a macro-PARP ADP-ribosyltransferase, but identity is low and immune roles are not shown here.

name_verdict.reason: The best Swiss-Prot match is PARP14, and the PARP14-specific RRM domains and many macrodomains fit PARP14 better than PARP9, which has two macrodomains and an inactive PARP domain. The header name PARP9 has no recorded evidence, though both genes belong to the macro-PARP group.

one_line: Probable sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter of the SLC5A8/SLC5A12 group in the sodium:solute symporter family.
summary: Its best Swiss-Prot match is bovine SLC5A12 (SMCT2) at 35.3% identity over the full length of the protein. It also carries a sodium:solute symporter (SSF) Pfam domain. Together these suggest a plasma-membrane symporter that moves monocarboxylates such as lactate with sodium. The 29-member Botryllus cluster points to a large lineage-specific expansion, so the substrate and the correspondence to a single vertebrate paralog are uncertain.
confidence_reason: A full-length match at 35% identity and a matching Pfam domain support the transporter family, but not the exact gene or substrate.

name_verdict.reason: The proposed name SLC5A12 rests on a 35.3% identity match, which gives the family rather than the paralog. The header name SLC5A8 is the sister paralog and has no recorded evidence. The evidence cannot tell the two apart in a tunicate.

one_line: A serpin-family protein, probably a secreted serine protease inhibitor; its exact vertebrate counterpart is unknown.
summary: Pfam finds two Serpin domain hits, and the best Swiss-Prot match is an archaeal serpin-like protein, Thermococcus kodakarensis TK1782, at 30.9% identity over 69% of the protein. Together these place the protein in the serpin family but do not identify a specific gene. FANTASIA's nearest protein, Drosophila Spn77Ba, suggests an extracellular role in regulating protease cascades, for example the melanization defense response. That is a weak hint with no alignment behind it. Whether the protein actually inhibits proteases depends on an intact reactive centre loop, which this evidence cannot check.
confidence_reason: Pfam and a moderate Swiss-Prot match agree on the serpin family, but identity is low and inhibitory activity and targets are not supported directly.

name_verdict.reason: The header name SERPINI1 (neuroserpin) is a specific vertebrate paralog that nothing on the sheet supports; the best match is an archaeal serpin at 31% identity. The proposed name 'Uncharacterized' only copies that archaeal entry's name and ignores the clear Serpin domains.

one_line: Probable secreted calcium-dependent phospholipase A2 of the group I/II family.
summary: It has a Phospholip_A2_1 Pfam domain. Its best Swiss-Prot match is cobra natratoxin, a group I secreted phospholipase A2, at 39.4% identity over 55% of the protein. This supports calcium-dependent hydrolysis of the sn-2 ester bond of phospholipids outside the cell, which releases fatty acids such as arachidonate. The toxin and potassium-channel keywords belong to the snake venom protein and should not be carried over. At 230 residues the protein is longer than a typical secreted PLA2, and about half of it has no match, so its extra regions are of unknown function.
confidence_reason: The domain and a moderate-identity match agree on secreted PLA2 activity, but the match covers only about half of the protein and does not identify the specific gene.

name_verdict.reason: PLA2G1B is one specific vertebrate paralog, and 39% identity to a snake group I enzyme cannot pick it out from the other group I/II/V/X secreted PLA2s. The proposed name 'Acidic' is a truncated fragment of the snake toxin's name, not a gene name.

one_line: Probable zinc-dependent beta-keto L-gulonate decarboxylase, the vertebrate ester hydrolase C11orf54 homolog.
summary: Its best Swiss-Prot match is rat Bkgd at 50.2% identity over 95% of the protein, and it has the DUF1907 domain typical of this family. Function therefore probably carries over: a zinc-binding enzyme that decarboxylates dehydro-L-gulonate, which also shows ester hydrolase activity. It probably acts in the cytoplasm and nucleus. The rat entry's roles in the DNA damage response and DNA repair regulation are less well established and are uncertain here. No activity has been measured for the Botryllus protein.
confidence_reason: About 50% identity over nearly the full length to a characterized enzyme, with a matching family domain.

name_verdict.reason: The proposed name Bkgd rests on 50% identity over 95% of the protein to rat Bkgd. The header 'ESTER' probably comes from the older name 'ester hydrolase C11orf54' for the same protein, but it is not a usable gene name.

one_line: Probable plasma-membrane sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter of the SLC5 family, SMCT-like.
summary: Its best Swiss-Prot match is bovine SLC5A12 (SMCT2) at 35.5% identity over 97% of the protein, and it has a sodium:solute symporter (SSF) Pfam domain. This supports a multi-pass plasma-membrane symporter that couples sodium to the uptake of solutes, possibly monocarboxylates such as lactate. At this identity the match gives the SLC5 family, and only tentatively the SMCT subgroup. The substrate is not certain. The protein belongs to an MMseqs2 cluster of 29 Botryllus proteins, which points to a lineage-specific expansion with no one-to-one match to either vertebrate gene.
confidence_reason: A full-length match and the SSF domain support a sodium symporter, but 35% identity does not settle the substrate or the paralog.

name_verdict.reason: SLC5A8 (SMCT1) and SLC5A12 (SMCT2) are paralogs from the vertebrate duplications. A 35.5% match to SLC5A12 cannot separate them, especially within a 29-member Botryllus expansion. The family name is the best supported.

one_line: Probable SLC5-family sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter, possibly truncated or a partial gene model.
summary: Its best Swiss-Prot match is human SLC5A12 (SMCT2) at 39.3% identity over 92% of the protein. This suggests a plasma-membrane sodium-coupled symporter, possibly for monocarboxylates such as lactate. The match gives the family, not the exact gene. At 418 residues it is shorter than typical SLC5 transporters of about 600 residues, and no Pfam domain passed the threshold. It may be a fragment or partial model, so whether it can transport anything is uncertain.
confidence_reason: A moderate-identity match over most of its length supports SLC5 family membership, but there is no domain support, the protein may be truncated, and the substrate is not established.

name_verdict.reason: SLC5A8 and SLC5A12 are vertebrate paralogs. A 39% match to SLC5A12 does not distinguish them in a tunicate, so the evidence supports only the shared family name.

one_line: A GLUT-family membrane transporter that probably moves hexose sugars across the plasma membrane.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is horse GLUT5 (SLC2A5), a fructose transporter, at 42% identity over the full protein. That points to a facilitated hexose transporter in the plasma membrane. Members of the GLUT family share about this much identity with one another, so the match gives the family, not the specific gene or substrate (glucose vs. fructose). No Pfam domain passed the gathering threshold, which is odd for this family. It sits in a 21-member Botryllus cluster whose members are named SLC2A5 or SLC2A7, so the GLUT family has expanded in this genome.
confidence_reason: Full-length match at 42% identity supports GLUT-family sugar transport, but the substrate and the specific gene are not resolved.

name_verdict.reason: The best match is GLUT5 (SLC2A5) at 42% identity over the whole protein. Nothing on the sheet supports the header name SLC2A1 (GLUT1) specifically. But 42% is within the range shared by many GLUT paralogs, so SLC2A5 is not established either, and the family name is the safer choice.

one_line: Probably a class A GPCR fragment, distantly related to leucine-rich-repeat hormone receptors; its ligand is unknown.
summary: A 7tm_1 Pfam domain marks this as a rhodopsin-like (class A) G protein-coupled receptor, which would sit in the plasma membrane. Its Swiss-Prot match is the snail receptor GRL101 at 29% identity over 57% of the protein. GRL101 is a leucine-rich-repeat GPCR, but that weak, partial match gives only the broad family. At 247 amino acids the protein is short for an LGR-type receptor and may be a fragment or a partial gene model. The ligand and downstream signaling cannot be inferred.
confidence_reason: GPCR membership rests on a Pfam domain, but the only homolog is weak and partial, and the ligand is unknown.

name_verdict.reason: The header name LRP5L (an LDL receptor-related protein) has no support on the sheet: there are no LDL-receptor domains, and both the Pfam domain and the best match are GPCRs. The proposed name 'G-like' is a truncated label, not a usable gene name, though it does reflect the GPCR match.

one_line: A semaphorin, probably a cell-surface guidance cue that signals through plexin receptors.
summary: A Sema Pfam domain places this protein in the semaphorin family. Semaphorins act as cell-surface or secreted cues that signal through plexins in axon guidance and cell migration. Its Swiss-Prot match is C. elegans Semaphorin-1A (smp-1), a transmembrane semaphorin, at 25.5% identity over 57% of the protein. That match supports the family but not the class. Whether it is a class 6-type transmembrane semaphorin, as the header name implies, is not resolved. It clusters with two neighbouring Botryllus genes that were annotated as SEMA6C or Sema3d-like.
confidence_reason: The Sema domain firmly gives the family, but the identity is low and the semaphorin class is uncertain.

name_verdict.reason: The Sema domain supports both SEMA6A and smp-1-like as semaphorins. But the only match is a nematode class 1 semaphorin at 25.5% identity over part of the protein, which can tell apart neither class 6 nor class 1. The family name is better supported.

one_line: An RBR-type E3 ubiquitin ligase, the single Botryllus counterpart of vertebrate RNF19A and RNF19B.
summary: Its Pfam domains (two IBR domains, IBR_1 and RBR_HH) define a RING-between-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase. Its Swiss-Prot match, pig RNF19A (Dorfin), at 54% identity over 59% of the protein, supports membership of the RNF19 subfamily. By homology, it probably ubiquitinates substrate proteins and may be membrane-associated, like RNF19A. Which vertebrate paralog it corresponds to cannot be decided, and the roughly 40% of the protein outside the match is uncharacterized.
confidence_reason: The RBR domain set and over 50% identity to RNF19A agree on an RNF19-type E3 ubiquitin ligase.

name_verdict.reason: The best match is RNF19A at 54% identity over 59% of the protein, and the header name is RNF19B. These are vertebrate paralogs, and one tunicate gene probably corresponds to both, so the evidence cannot choose between them. The subfamily name RNF19 is recommended.

one_line: A cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, probably in the ER, distantly related to the vertebrate CYP3A enzymes.
summary: A p450 Pfam domain and a full-length match to hamster CYP3A31 (35.7% identity, 100% coverage) make this a heme-containing cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. Like CYP3A enzymes, it probably sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and oxidizes steroids or foreign compounds. At this identity the match gives the broad CYP3-like family. The substrates, including the testosterone 6-beta-hydroxylase activity annotated on the hamster enzyme, cannot be carried over. It belongs to a 73-member Botryllus P450 cluster whose members carry assorted CYP2 and CYP3 names, so P450s have expanded in this lineage.
confidence_reason: P450 monooxygenase function is well supported, but at 36% identity the family assignment is approximate and the substrate is unknown.

name_verdict.reason: CYP3A4 (human) and CYP3A31 (hamster) are both CYP3A subfamily members. At 35.7% identity, neither specific gene can be supported for a tunicate P450. The family-level name is the best fit.

one_line: Probably a sodium-coupled solute symporter of the SLC5 family, related to SLC5A8 and SLC5A12.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match, mouse Slc5a12 (sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter 2), is at 36.5% identity over 99% of the protein. A sodium:solute symporter family (SSF) domain is also present. Together these point to a plasma-membrane transporter that moves a solute together with sodium, possibly lactate or other monocarboxylates. At this identity the exact substrate and the vertebrate counterpart (SLC5A8 or SLC5A12) are uncertain. It belongs to a cluster of 29 similar Botryllus proteins, which suggests a lineage-specific expansion.
confidence_reason: A full-length match at 36.5% identity and an SSF domain support the family and sodium-coupled transport, but not the specific substrate.

name_verdict.reason: SLC5A8 and SLC5A12 are close vertebrate paralogs. The best match, mouse Slc5a12, is at only 36.5% identity, which supports the family but not one paralog over the other. Tunicates predate the split, so the family name fits best.

one_line: A protein kinase with a death domain, probably involved in death-domain signaling such as RIPK1 or IRAK.
summary: Pfam finds a protein kinase domain (Pkinase, PK_Tyr_Ser-Thr) and a death domain. The Swiss-Prot match, mouse Ankk1 at 33.2% identity over 53% of the protein, probably covers only the kinase domain. Ankk1 has ankyrin repeats, not a death domain. jackhmmer from an IRAK4 seed (E 2e-47) and the FANTASIA hint (nearest protein mouse RIPK1, weak evidence without alignment) both point to death-domain kinases that act in innate immune, inflammatory or cell-death signaling. Which of these families it belongs to, and whether it is active as a kinase, is not resolved.
confidence_reason: The kinase and death-domain architecture is clear, but no sequence match identifies the family or the pathway.

name_verdict.reason: RIPK2 has a CARD rather than a death domain, and no hit supports RIPK2 specifically. Ankk1 is the best Swiss-Prot hit, but only at 33% over half the protein, and Ankk1 has ankyrin repeats, not the death domain found here. The domain makeup fits RIPK1 or IRAK better, but no hit supports a specific gene.

one_line: A putative serine/threonine protein kinase whose family and function are unclear.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match, mouse sperm motility kinase 2B (Smok2b) at 30.0% identity over 56% of the protein, and jackhmmer hits from IRAK4 and JAK3 seeds (E 1e-55 and 1e-47) point to a protein kinase domain. No Pfam domain reaches the gathering threshold, so the kinase domain may be divergent, and whether it is catalytically active is unknown. Smok genes are rodent sperm kinases, so the match gives only a general kinase relationship. Nothing on the sheet indicates its pathway or where it acts.
confidence_reason: Only moderate, partial similarity to kinases, and no Pfam domain at the threshold.

name_verdict.reason: IRE1 would need a luminal sensor domain and a C-terminal RNase (KEN) domain, and no evidence on the sheet shows these. Smok2b is a rodent-specific sperm kinase matched at only 30% over 56% of the protein, so it is not a credible ortholog. The evidence supports only a generic kinase name.

one_line: Probably an S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase with an unknown substrate.
summary: Several Pfam methyltransferase domains (Methyltransf_11, _12, _23, _25, _31, Ubie_methyltran) and the Swiss-Prot match, a putative methyltransferase from Dictyostelium at 28.5% identity over 62% of the protein, point to a class I SAM-dependent methyltransferase. The substrate and the cell location cannot be inferred from this evidence. The single PAC4 domain hit has no clear meaning here.
confidence_reason: Consistent methyltransferase domains support the enzyme class, but the low-identity match to an uncharacterized protein gives no substrate.

name_verdict.reason: No hit on the sheet supports TMT1 (thiol or trans-aconitate methyltransferase) specifically. The proposed 'Putative-like' comes from parsing a 'Putative methyltransferase' description and is not a gene name. Only the methyltransferase class is supported.

one_line: A caspase-family cysteine protease with a death domain, probably an initiator caspase in apoptosis.
summary: Pfam finds a caspase catalytic domain (Peptidase_C14) and a death domain. The Swiss-Prot match, chicken caspase-2 at 29.4% identity over 54% of the protein, and a strong jackhmmer hit from a CASP1 seed (E 9e-86) place it in the caspase family. The domain makeup, a protein-interaction domain before the protease, suggests an initiator caspase that is activated in a signaling complex and cleaves other caspases during apoptosis. FANTASIA's nearest protein, fly Dronc, fits this, but it is only a weak hint. The vertebrate counterpart is uncertain: CASP2 has a CARD rather than a death domain, and the cluster members carry mixed names (CASP1, CASP2, CASP8, CASP14), which suggests a tunicate-specific caspase expansion.
confidence_reason: The caspase domain and caspase-family hits are consistent, but identity is low and the catalytic residues were not checked.

name_verdict.reason: 'CASPL2' is not a standard gene symbol and is ambiguous. 'CASP2-like' reflects the best Swiss-Prot hit, caspase-2 at 29% identity, and the '-like' suffix correctly flags that only the family is supported.

one_line: Papain-family cysteine protease of the cathepsin L subfamily, probably a lysosomal protein-degrading enzyme.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is Aedes aegypti cathepsin L-like peptidase at 54% identity over the whole protein. That match, plus the Peptidase_C1 and Inhibitor_I29 domains, points to a cathepsin L-type cysteine protease. It is likely made as an inactive zymogen whose propeptide (Inhibitor_I29) is removed to activate it. It probably degrades proteins in lysosomes or endosomes. Its MMseqs2 cluster also holds proteins named CTSL, CTSV, CTSS and CTSH, so Botryllus has several related cathepsins, and which vertebrate cathepsin L-type paralog this one matches is not settled.
confidence_reason: A full-length match at 54% identity and matching Pfam domains support a cathepsin L-type cysteine protease, but not one specific vertebrate paralog.

name_verdict.reason: The 54% full-length match to a cathepsin L-like peptidase supports the header name CTSL at the subfamily level. The proposed name 'Cathepsin' is correct but vague. It covers cysteine, serine and aspartic cathepsins. '-like' is added because vertebrate CTSL and CTSV cannot be told apart at this identity.

one_line: Rab33 small GTPase, likely regulating Golgi membrane traffic and autophagy.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is Ciona intestinalis putative Rab-33 at 71% identity over 89% of the protein, which supports Rab33 at the gene level. The Ras-superfamily Pfam domains (Ras, Arf, Roc, MMR_HSR1, Gtr1_RagA) all reflect one small-GTPase domain. In vertebrates, Rab33 proteins act at the Golgi in retrograde transport and in autophagosome formation. The Ciona entry also lists the plasma membrane and prenylation. Vertebrates have RAB33A and RAB33B, and this single tunicate gene probably corresponds to both.
confidence_reason: A 71% identity match to a tunicate Rab33 over most of the protein supports the gene identity, though its role in Botryllus is inferred from other species.

name_verdict.reason: The 71% match to Ciona Rab-33 supports the header name RAB33B at the gene level. The paralog letter B is not supported, because tunicates likely have one gene for RAB33A and RAB33B. The proposed name 'Putative' is a parsing artifact, not a gene name.

one_line: Core histone H4, part of the nucleosome that packages DNA into chromatin.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is Oikopleura dioica histone H4 at 100% identity over the full length. Its 103-residue length fits histone H4. It is a core nucleosome component in the nucleus, and its tail is a known target of acetylation and methylation. The CENP-T_C and TAF Pfam hits are histone-fold domains, not separate functions. It sits in a cluster of 18 Botryllus proteins, consistent with a multi-copy histone gene family.
confidence_reason: An identical full-length match to tunicate histone H4, one of the most conserved proteins known, leaves little doubt.

name_verdict.reason: The 100% identity match to histone H4 supports the proposed name, though 'H4.1' is just one of several Oikopleura gene copy names, so 'histone H4' is recommended. The header name HIST1H3D is a histone H3 gene and is wrong for this protein.

one_line: Kelch-repeat protein of the kelch-like (KLHL) family. Its exact gene and function are unclear.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is human KLHL23 at 23.8% identity over 56% of the protein, which shows only that part of it is related to kelch-like proteins. Two Kelch_1 repeats were found. No BTB domain was detected, so it is unclear whether it works as a Cul3 ubiquitin ligase substrate adaptor like typical KLHL proteins. Its MMseqs2 cluster holds many proteins named after different KLHL genes and ENC1, which fits a family assignment only.
confidence_reason: A weak partial match below 25% identity and kelch repeats alone support only the kelch-like family, not a specific gene or function.

name_verdict.reason: The match to KLHL23 is at 23.8% identity over 56% of the protein, too weak to support KLHL23 specifically. The header name KLHL36 has no recorded support beyond the family. Both are kelch-like family members, and the evidence cannot tell which, if either, this is.

card_name: KAP family P-loop NTPase domain-containing protein (putative)
one_line: Distant relative of Kidins220/NKPD1-type proteins. Its function is unknown.
summary: Its Swiss-Prot match is zebrafish Kidins220b at 22.2% identity over 96% of the protein (E-value 1.6e-26). This suggests distant relatedness along its length but does not support the gene identity. No Pfam domain passed the threshold, so the ankyrin repeats and transmembrane features of Kidins220 are not confirmed here.
